blocks.text: In the fourth verse, What the gazam left, the arbe has eaten, and what the arbe left, the jelek has eaten, and what the jelek left, the chasil has eaten.] These are four species of locusts, as [III, 290] we noted earlier ^{a)}, which we call here by their Hebrew names because Latin ones are not available. So too below, in chapter 2, verse 25: And I will restore to you the years which the ARBE, IELEK, CHASIL and GAZAM have eaten. There gazam, which had been first, is named last. This should be noted against the Hebrews, who think that these four species of locusts laid waste Judaea in four successive years: the gazam in the first year, the arbe in the second, the jelek in the third, and finally the chasil in the fourth. To me this seems hardly probable. For if the locust called gazam had been sent into Judaea in the first year, it would not be placed last in Ioel II, 25. And in enumerating these plagues the Prophet would have kept the same order in both places. Moreover, if each species had been assigned to a single year, it would not be said that the arbe ate what the gazam left, and the jelek what the arbe left, and the chasil what the jelek left. For this year's produce is not the remainder of the previous year's, nor can what will grow in the coming year be counted among this year's remains. Therefore, whether this plague of locusts lasted one year or, as seems rightly concluded from Ioel II, 25., extended over several years, I think that the individual species of locusts are not to be assigned to individual years, but that all of them fell upon Judaea in the same year. Thus, as one swarm left a field, another followed, to graze off and consume the remains of the preceding one, if any were left; and this was repeated as often as necessary, until nothing at all remained in the field on which either men or beasts could feed. Nor do I any more approve of their claim that this Judaean plague differed from the Egyptian in that a single kind of locust (namely ארבה arbe) fell upon Egypt, but those four species upon Judaea. For although arbe is taken εἰδικῶς [eidikōs] for a particular species of locust when it is set against the others, as in Joel and Levit. XI, 21., yet it is mostly used γενικῶς [genikōs] for the whole genus of locusts. So Moses took it when he dealt with the arbe sent upon the Egyptians, so that ילק jelek and חסיל chasil and other species of locusts were also included. Accordingly David says of the Egyptians, Psal. LXXVIII, 46.: He gave their produce to the chasil, and their labour to the arbe. And Psal. CV, 34.: He spoke, and the arbe came, and the jelek without number. Thus not the arbe alone, but also the chasil and the jelek were sent by God against them. Rightly, then, in Pisides God arrays against the Egyptians παγγενῆ τὴν ἀκρίδα [pangenē tēn akrida], the locust of every kind. How the Chaldeans, Syrians and Arabs render the four species of locusts in Joel, gazam, arbe, jelek and chasil, [col. 466] is of no concern here. In the Greek and the Vulgate they are ἡ κάμπη [hē kampē], ἡ ἀκρὶς [hē akris], ὁ βροῦχος [ho brouchos], ἡ ἐρυσίβη [hē erysibē]: eruca [caterpillar], locusta [locust], bruchus [bruchus], rubigo [blight]. Of these the first and the last do not belong to the genus of locusts. For ἡ ἐρυσίβη [hē erysibē], rubigo [blight], is not even an animal, but a disease of crops. We therefore by no means stand by this version. For we are fully persuaded [III, 291] that the four Hebrew words signify four species of locusts. This all the Hebrews assert here with one voice, although they cannot define how those species differ from one another.
